concept.name: Reversal
concept.definition: A durable change in the direction of the prevailing trend — an uptrend turning into a downtrend or vice versa — as opposed to a temporary counter-move. In chart analysis, reversals are confirmed through structure (broken swing sequences, broken trendlines, completed reversal patterns), and only after the fact with certainty.
concept.intuition: The tide actually turns: what was a staircase up becomes a staircase down.
concept.mechanics: Read from structure shifts: in an uptrend, a lower high followed by a lower low (breaking the last higher low) signals a possible reversal; trendline breaks, support/resistance breaks, and classical reversal patterns (double tops/bottoms, head and shoulders) provide corroboration. Depth and duration distinguish reversal from pullback or consolidation.
concept.failure_modes: Early reversal signals frequently turn out to be deep pullbacks; acting on the first structural break exposes the trader to trend resumption.
concept.misconceptions: That reversals can be called at the turn; every real-time 'reversal call' is a probabilistic bet, and counter-trend calling is a classic account destroyer.
concept.example: An uptrend printing 55, 58 highs and 52, 54 lows breaks down through 54, then rallies only to 56 (lower high) and falls under 52: the reversed sequence confirms a trend change.

citations.source: Fenefx — What Is a Price Correction or Pullback?
citations.section: The Difference Between Pullback, Trend Reversal, and Price Consolidation
